subject: Mass Media / Mass Communication (Code: 318)
past_paper_reference: CUET UG Mass Media Past Papers (2022-2024)

questions.sub_topic: Diffusion of Innovations: Five Adopter Categories (Rogers, 1962)
questions.question: In Everett Rogers' 'Diffusion of Innovations' theory, which adopter category represents the pragmatic 34% of a population that adopts an innovation just before the average citizen, requiring proven utility?
options: A) Early Majority
B) Innovators
C) Early Adopters
D) Laggards
questions.explanation: Rogers' adoption bell curve: Innovators (2.5%), Early Adopters (13.5%), Early Majority (34%), Late Majority (34%), and Laggards (16%).

questions.sub_topic: Third-Person Effect: W. Phillips Davison (1983)
questions.question: In mass communication psychology, what does W. Phillips Davison's 'Third-Person Effect' hypothesis predict about human perception?
options: A) Viewers can only comprehend a television news broadcast if three people watch it together
B) Individuals tend to believe that mass media messages have a greater negative or persuasive impact on other people ('them') than on themselves ('me')
C) Audiences believe that all third-party commercial advertisements are completely truthful
D) Individuals believe that computer algorithms have zero influence on anyone in society
questions.explanation: Davison demonstrated that people systematically overestimate media influence on others while underestimating its influence on themselves, often motivating support for censorship.

questions.sub_topic: Harold Innis: Empire and Communications (Time-Biased vs Space-Biased Media, 1950)
questions.question: In economic historian Harold Innis's media ecology landmark 'Empire and Communications' (1950), how do 'Time-Biased' media shape social institutions compared to 'Space-Biased' media?
options: A) Time-biased media travel faster than the speed of light, while space-biased media operate only in dark rooms
B) Time-biased media can only be read at night, while space-biased media operate exclusively in the daytime

C) Time-biased media (stone, clay, parchment) are durable and heavy, favoring decentralized, religious, and tradition-bound cultures; Space-biased media (papyrus, cheap paper, radio) are light and portable, favoring vast administrative empires and secular political expansion
D) Time-biased media are prohibited by international treaties, while space-biased media are funded by banks
questions.explanation: Innis argued the material bias of communication media structures civilizations: durable heavy media foster enduring religious hierarchies (time bias); light portable media enable imperial administrative reach (space bias).

questions.sub_topic: Walter Benjamin: The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction (1936)
questions.question: In his seminal 1936 cultural essay, what did Walter Benjamin argue is lost when an original work of art is subjected to mass technological reproduction (such as photography and cinema)?
options: A) Its physical chemical molecular structure and electrical conductivity
B) Its ability to be bought and sold for monetary paper currency in commercial markets
C) Its optical visibility to human beings who do not wear eyeglasses
D) Its 'Aura'—its unique presence in time and space, authenticity, and historic embeddedness in traditional ritual and cult value
questions.explanation: Benjamin showed that mechanical reproduction strips art of its 'aura' (uniqueness and cult/ritual embeddedness), emancipating art from ritual to function as a democratic, politicized practice.

questions.sub_topic: Roland Barthes: Mythologies and Ex-nomination (1957)
questions.question: In 'Mythologies' (1957), how does Roland Barthes explain the ideological function of bourgeois 'Myth' in mass culture?
options: A) Myth transforms contingent, historical, and class-constructed reality into timeless, unquestioned 'nature', making bourgeois cultural values appear as universal, natural common sense
B) Myth translates ancient Greek fairy tales into modern mathematical computer algorithms
C) Myth forces all print newspapers to publish fictional astrological horoscopes on front pages
D) Myth is an obsolete medieval superstition that was eradicated by industrial steam printing
questions.explanation: Barthes demonstrated that modern myth depoliticizes culture: taking historical, contingent bourgeois norms and naturalizing them as universal, unquestionable reality.

questions.sub_topic: Ferdinand de Saussure: Arbitrariness of the Sign and Value (1916)
questions.question: In Ferdinand de Saussure's foundational linguistics ('Course in General Linguistics', 1916), what does the principle of the 'Arbitrariness of the Sign' fundamentally establish?
options: A) Words can only be spoken by individuals who hold authorized certificates in grammar

B) There is no natural, intrinsic, or necessary physical link between the Signifier (sound-image/word) and the Signified (mental concept); the relationship is purely conventional and socially constructed
C) All human languages share identical dictionary vocabulary words and pronunciations
D) Written words have physical weight in grams that can be weighed on mechanical scales
questions.explanation: Saussure established that the bond between signifier (e.g., the letters/sounds 'c-a-t') and signified (concept of a feline) is arbitrary, sustained purely by cultural and linguistic convention.

questions.sub_topic: Edward Herman & Noam Chomsky: Five Filters of Manufacturing Consent (1988)
questions.question: In Edward S. Herman and Noam Chomsky's Propaganda Model ('Manufacturing Consent', 1988), which five structural institutional filters systematically screen and shape elite mass media news?
options: A) 1) Literacy rates; 2) Printing press speed; 3) Paper quality; 4) Postal rates; 5) Reader intelligence
B) 1) Camera lenses; 2) Microphone frequencies; 3) Studio lighting; 4) Editing software; 5) Screen resolution

C) 1) Size, ownership concentration, and profit orientation; 2) Advertising as primary income source; 3) Reliance on government and corporate sources; 4) Flak as disciplinary mechanism; 5) Anti-communism (or dominant enemy ideology)
D) 1) Radio towers; 2) Fiber cables; 3) Satellites; 4) Submarines; 5) Telegraph wires
questions.explanation: Herman & Chomsky's 5 filters explain how elite consensus is manufactured structurally without overt conspiracy: corporate ownership, advertising reliance, official sourcing, flak, and dominant enemy framing.

questions.sub_topic: Byline Definition
questions.question: The printed line appearing at the beginning of a published news article or investigative feature stating the reporter or writer's name is the:
options: A) Dateline
B) Masthead
C) Cutline
D) Byline
questions.explanation: A byline credits the author of the article, establishing individual journalistic accountability and ownership.

questions.sub_topic: Embargo in Journalistic Sourcing
questions.question: In professional journalism, when an institution releases a press report or scientific study to journalists under a strict 'Embargo', what does this ethical agreement mandate?
options: A) Reporters receive advance access to review and prepare the story, but are strictly forbidden from publishing or broadcasting it until a specified future date and time
B) The news organization is permanently banned from ever publishing the story
C) The reporter must pay a financial licensing fee before opening the document
D) The government police seize the reporter's computers and tape recorders
questions.explanation: A press embargo gives journalists advance access to complex material (e.g., scientific papers, budgets) so they can research thoroughly before a coordinated release time.

questions.sub_topic: Proofreading vs Copy Editing
questions.question: In publication workflows, what distinguishes 'Proofreading' from earlier 'Copy Editing'?
options: A) Proofreading is done before an article is written, while copy editing is done after it is printed

B) Copy editing polishes prose, checks facts, and rewrites structure on raw copy; Proofreading is the final quality check on formatted proofs to catch typographical, layout, and typesetting errors before press
C) Proofreading involves selling commercial advertising space, while copy editing involves reporting
D) Proofreading is performed exclusively by computer algorithms, while copy editing is done by interns
questions.explanation: Copy editing refines language, clarity, and factual accuracy in draft text; proofreading is the final audit of typeset pages to catch typographical, visual, and layout errors before printing.

questions.sub_topic: Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985): Custom Duty on Newsprint
questions.question: In 'Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India' (1985), what seminal doctrine did the Supreme Court establish regarding government taxation on the press?
options: A) Newspapers are completely exempt from paying any taxes, utility bills, or postal charges
B) The government possesses unlimited power to levy any tax on newspapers without judicial interference

C) While newspapers are subject to ordinary general taxation, fiscal levies that are excessive, burdensome, and directly designed to restrict newspaper circulation or cripple the press violate Article 19(1)(a)
D) Customs duties can only be imposed on imported electronic computers and never on physical paper
questions.explanation: Justice Venkataramiah held that taxation cannot be weaponized against the press: fiscal imposts that impose a crippling burden on circulation breach Article 19(1)(a).

questions.sub_topic: R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu (Auto Shankar Case, 1994)
questions.question: In the landmark 'Auto Shankar Case' ('R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu', 1994), what historic rule did the Supreme Court lay down balancing the Right to Privacy and Press Freedom?
options: A) All autobiographies written by prisoners must be shredded and burned by jail authorities
B) Public officials hold an absolute right to prevent newspapers from mentioning their names
C) The right to privacy completely supersedes press freedom in every criminal investigation

D) The state cannot impose prior restraint on a newspaper publishing an autobiography; once a matter becomes part of public records, the right to privacy no longer exists, and public officials cannot sue for libel without proving actual malice
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court recognized the right to privacy (under Article 21) but held public officials cannot suppress publication of public record matters or obtain prior injunctions without proving Sullivan-standard actual malice.

questions.sub_topic: Vernacular Press Act, 1878 (The Gagging Act): Lord Lytton's Censorship
questions.question: Why did the colonial administration under Viceroy Lord Lytton enact the notorious Vernacular Press Act, 1878 (derided as 'The Gagging Act'), and how did Amrita Bazar Patrika outmaneuver it?
options: A) The Act imposed discriminatory pre-censorship and heavy security bonds exclusively on Indian-language newspapers; Amrita Bazar Patrika outwitted Lytton by converting overnight from Bengali into an English-language weekly
B) The Act banned all printing presses from operating within twenty miles of Calcutta; the paper moved to London
C) The Act required all newspapers to be written in Persian; Amrita Bazar Patrika translated all editions into French
D) The Act nationalized all Indian newspapers; the publishers surrendered the printing presses to colonial police
questions.explanation: Lytton's 1878 Act discriminated against vernacular papers; Sisir Kumar Ghosh transformed Amrita Bazar Patrika into an English paper overnight, evading the law since English papers were exempt.

questions.sub_topic: Jürgen Habermas: The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962)
questions.question: In his foundational 1962 thesis, Jürgen Habermas traced the degeneration of the 18th-century bourgeois public sphere (salons, coffeehouses, independent press) into a state of decay in the 20th century because:
options: A) Coffeehouses and cafes were permanently shut down by municipal public health ordinances

B) A critical, reasoning public engaging in rational-critical debate was transformed by corporate commercialism, PR, and consumer capitalism into a passive, atomized audience consuming mass entertainment
C) The invention of the steam locomotive physically prevented citizens from gathering in towns
D) The public sphere was legally restricted to citizens who held patents in mechanical engineering
questions.explanation: Habermas demonstrated that commercialization and public relations transformed the public sphere from a space of rational-critical debate into a manufactured realm of consumer publicity and political marketing.

questions.sub_topic: Brand Extension Strategy
questions.question: In brand marketing, what is a 'Brand Extension' strategy?
options: A) Physically enlarging the dimensions of a corporate logo on a billboard by five hundred percent
B) Extending the payment deadline of an advertising agency's commercial client by ninety days
C) Using an established, successful brand name to launch a new product in an entirely different product category (e.g., Caterpillar construction launching rugged work boots)
D) A legal lawsuit extending the copyright protection of a commercial television commercial
questions.explanation: Brand extension leverages established brand equity and consumer trust to introduce products into a new category, reducing marketing launch costs.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Public Relations
questions.sub_topic: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) in India (Companies Act, 2013)
questions.question: Under Section 135 of the Indian Companies Act, 2013, what statutory CSR mandate is imposed on qualifying profitable corporations?
options: A) They must donate fifty percent of their manufactured commercial products to foreign embassies
B) They must run corporate television advertisements praising government ministries every month
C) They must employ ten percent of their workforce in professional athletic sports teams
D) They must spend at least 2% of their average net profits over the preceding three financial years on approved social development, education, environmental, and healthcare projects
questions.explanation: India was the first country to mandate statutory CSR: Section 135 requires qualifying companies to invest 2% of average 3-year net profits into approved Schedule VII social initiatives.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Advertising Theory
questions.sub_topic: Jean Baudrillard: Consumer Society and Sign-Value (1970)
questions.question: In 'The Consumer Society' (1970) and 'For a Critique of the Political Economy of the Sign' (1972), Jean Baudrillard argued that modern advertising has transformed commodities so that consumers primarily consume:
options: A) 'Sign-Value'—the social prestige, status, identity, and lifestyle connotations manufactured by advertising, completely eclipsing the object's physical Marxian use-value and exchange-value
B) Physical raw metals and chemical compounds synthesized in manufacturing factories
C) Handwritten letters signed by corporate advertising agency art directors
D) Astronomical calculations mapping planetary orbits around the sun
questions.explanation: Baudrillard demonstrated that in late capitalism, commodities are consumed for 'sign-value'—symbolic prestige and social differentiation structured through advertising—rather than utilitarian function.

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Advertising Classics
questions.sub_topic: Rosser Reeves: Reality in Advertising and Unique Selling Proposition (1961)
questions.question: In his influential 1961 manifesto 'Reality in Advertising', Ted Bates agency chairman Rosser Reeves insisted that an effective Unique Selling Proposition (USP) must meet which three uncompromising rules?
options: A) 1) Use humor; 2) Feature a celebrity actor; 3) Change the slogan every week

B) 1) Each ad must make a specific proposition to the consumer; 2) The proposition must be one that the competition cannot or does not offer; 3) The proposition must be so strong that it can move the mass millions
C) 1) Be printed in color; 2) Use rhyming poetry; 3) Avoid mentioning product prices
D) 1) Run on television; 2) Run on radio; 3) Be approved by municipal government censors
questions.explanation: Reeves formulated the 3 pillars of a USP: concrete proposition ('buy X, get Y benefit'), uniqueness (competitor cannot or does not offer it), and pulling power (strong enough to drive mass sales).

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: PR Models
questions.sub_topic: James Grunig & Todd Hunt: Four Models of Public Relations (1984)
questions.question: In their seminal PR framework (1984), which of Grunig and Hunt's Four Models of Public Relations relies on one-way dissemination of information from organization to publics where truth is essential, but without reciprocal audience feedback research?
options: A) The Press Agentry / Publicity Model
B) The Two-Way Asymmetrical Model
C) The Public Information Model
D) The Two-Way Symmetrical Model
questions.explanation: Grunig & Hunt's 4 models: Press Agentry (propaganda/hype, truth not essential), Public Information (one-way factual dissemination, truth essential, like Ivy Lee), Two-Way Asymmetrical (scientific persuasion), and Two-Way Symmetrical (dialogue/mutual adjustment).

questions.topic: Advertising and Public Relations: Consumer Protection Law
questions.sub_topic: Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) Guidelines on Misleading Ads (2022)
questions.question: Under the 'Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements for Misleading Advertisements' (2022) issued by the CCPA in India, what liability is imposed on celebrity endorsers?
options: A) Celebrity endorsers are completely immune from any legal liability or financial fines
B) Celebrity endorsers must personally manufacture every product they advertise in their own home
C) Celebrity endorsers are prohibited from receiving any financial compensation for commercial ads

D) Endorsers must carry out mandatory due diligence to reflect their genuine and reasonably current opinion, and can be barred from endorsing any product for up to one to three years for participating in misleading advertisements
questions.explanation: The 2022 CCPA guidelines hold celebrity endorsers legally accountable: requiring due diligence and empowering authorities to impose fines and bans up to 3 years for deceptive endorsements.

questions.sub_topic: Pedestal Camera Movement
questions.question: In a television studio, what physical camera adjustment occurs when the director calls to 'Pedestal Up' (Ped Up)?
options: A) The entire camera apparatus is raised physically higher off the ground using the studio pedestal's pneumatic or hydraulic column, without changing the vertical tilt angle
B) The camera lens optical zoom is zoomed in to an extreme close-up of the actor's face
C) The camera is tilted vertically upward toward the ceiling on its pan-tilt head
D) The camera operator wheels the camera forward across the studio floor
questions.explanation: Pedestaling adjusts camera elevation vertically through the hydraulic pedestal column, changing eye level while keeping lens axis level.

questions.sub_topic: Timecode: SMPTE (Hours:Minutes:Seconds:Frames)
questions.question: In professional video post-production and broadcasting, what does 'SMPTE Timecode' provide to editors?
options: A) A measurement of the physical temperature of television camera electronic sensors
B) An exact, standardized electronic frame address stamped on every single video frame in the format HH:MM:SS:FF, enabling frame-accurate synchronization and editing
C) A digital code that counts the total number of words spoken in the television script
D) A cryptographic key that prevents viewers from recording broadcasts on home VCRs
questions.explanation: SMPTE timecode stamps every frame with Hours:Minutes:Seconds:Frames, providing frame-accurate precision for multi-track audio-video sync and non-linear editing.

questions.sub_topic: Chiaroscuro vs High-Key Lighting Aesthetics
questions.question: In dramatic television directing, how does 'High-Key Lighting' aesthetically differ from 'Low-Key Lighting' (Chiaroscuro)?
options: A) High-Key lighting uses only red light bulbs, while Low-Key lighting uses blue light bulbs
B) High-Key lighting is used exclusively outdoors, while Low-Key lighting is used only in submarines

C) High-Key lighting uses a low contrast ratio between key and fill lights, producing a bright, even illumination with virtually no deep shadows (common in sitcoms and news); Low-Key lighting uses high contrast with deep, dramatic shadows and dark backgrounds
D) High-Key lighting can only be viewed in black and white, while Low-Key lighting is in full color
questions.explanation: High-key features bright, uniform illumination with minimal shadows (low key-to-fill ratio, 1:1 or 2:1); low-key relies on high contrast and deep shadows (chiaroscuro, 8:1 or 16:1) for suspense.

questions.sub_topic: Inter-frame vs Intra-frame Compression (GOP, I-Frames, P-Frames, B-Frames)
questions.question: In digital television video compression codecs (such as MPEG-4 AVC / H.264), why are 'B-Frames' (Bi-directional predictive frames) able to achieve the highest data compression ratios?
options: A) They delete seventy percent of the pixels from every third line of video resolution
B) They record images exclusively in black and white and discard all color data
C) They contain complete, standalone uncompressed photographic image frames
D) They encode only temporal differences by referencing motion vectors and pixel changes from both preceding and succeeding reference frames (forward and backward prediction)
questions.explanation: In a Group of Pictures (GOP), I-frames are intra-coded (standalone); P-frames predict forward; B-frames use bidirectional temporal prediction (past and future), yielding maximum compression.

questions.sub_topic: Line Cutting / Live Switching Aesthetics
questions.question: During a live multi-camera television broadcast, what is the 'Line Cut' produced by the Technical Director under the Director's command?
options: A) The real-time, live-edited master video output switched dynamically between cameras and graphics as the event unfolds, recorded or transmitted directly to air
B) The physical severance of electrical copper wires when a storm strikes the studio
C) The script editing process where lines of dialogue are deleted by the teleprompter operator
D) A specialized transition where a laser beam cuts the television screen in half
questions.explanation: The line cut (or program mix) is the live switched broadcast stream executed in real time by the director and vision mixer, as opposed to isolated camera recordings (ISO feeds).

questions.sub_topic: Doordarshan National Programme and Krishi Darshan (1967)
questions.question: Launched on January 26, 1967 in collaboration with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and Department of Atomic Energy, which historic agricultural television program is Doordarshan's longest-running broadcast?
options: A) Hum Log
B) Krishi Darshan
C) Chitrahaar
D) Buniyaad
questions.explanation: Krishi Darshan commenced on January 26, 1967 to disseminate agricultural innovations to tele-clubs in rural villages around Delhi, standing as Indian television's longest-running development program.

questions.sub_topic: Cue Sheet in Radio Broadcasting
questions.question: A production document used by a radio presenter and audio engineer detailing the exact timing, track names, durations, and intro/outro cues for every recorded song and commercial is a:
options: A) Masthead
B) Slug
C) Cue sheet
D) Dateline
questions.explanation: A radio cue sheet lists timings, vocal intro lengths, track titles, and outro words, coordinating timing between on-air talent and audio operators.

questions.sub_topic: Audio Limiting vs Audio Compression
questions.question: In radio broadcast audio processing, at what compression ratio threshold does an audio dynamic processor transition from a 'Compressor' to a 'Limiter'?
options: A) When the compression ratio is set to 2:1
B) When the audio frequency is lowered below 20 Hertz
C) When the microphone is switched off by the sound engineer
D) When the compression ratio reaches 10:1 or infinity:1 (preventing the signal from exceeding the ceiling threshold under any circumstances)
questions.explanation: While compressors use gentle ratios (2:1 to 4:1) to smooth dynamics, a limiter uses aggressive ratios (10:1 or ∞:1) to act as a hard brickwall ceiling preventing peaks from clipping.

questions.sub_topic: Phone-In Radio Program Dynamics
questions.question: In interactive talk radio, why do broadcast stations maintain a mandatory 'Seven-Second Audio Delay' unit during live call-in shows?
options: A) To provide the broadcast engineer with a brief time buffer to dump or mute the audio line if a caller uses defamatory, obscene, or legally actionable language on live air
B) Because telephone signals take seven seconds to travel through satellite cables
C) To allow the presenter to consult a dictionary before answering every caller question
D) To translate spoken regional dialects into national standardized English language
questions.explanation: The profanity delay (dump button) buffers live caller audio by 7 seconds, giving producers time to cut off profanity or defamation before transmission reaches receiver antennas.

questions.sub_topic: AIR Code for Broadcast: Prohibited Content Categories
questions.question: Under the All India Radio (AIR) Code for Broadcast, which categories of content are strictly prohibited from being broadcast over state transmitters?
options: A) Any broadcast of classical Indian instrumental musical ragas
B) Criticism of friendly countries, attack on religion or communities, anything obscene or defamatory, incitement to violence, contempt of court, and aspersions against the President and Judiciary
C) Educational lectures analyzing scientific weather forecasts and rainfall data
D) Broadcasts describing agricultural crop farming techniques in vernacular dialects
questions.explanation: The AIR Broadcast Code strictly bars religious attacks, criticism of friendly nations, obscenity, defamation, incitement to violence, and contempt of court or constitutional offices.

questions.sub_topic: Reverberation Time (RT60) in Acoustic Engineering
questions.question: In acoustic engineering for broadcast radio studios, what does the standardized metric 'RT60' (Reverberation Time 60) measure?
options: A) The total number of minutes that a radio presenter can speak without drinking water
B) The physical distance in feet that sound waves travel before striking a studio microphone
C) The time required in seconds for the sound pressure level of an acoustic sound to decay by 60 decibels after the sound source has abruptly stopped
D) The electrical voltage consumed by radio broadcast transmitters operating at sixty hertz
questions.explanation: RT60 measures reverberance: the time required for sound reflections to decay by 60 dB. Voice studios require low RT60 (~0.2 to 0.4 seconds) for crisp, dry speech intelligibility.

questions.sub_topic: Proximity Effect in Directional Microphones
questions.question: In radio vocal broadcasting, what acoustic physical phenomenon causes a radio DJ's voice to sound unnaturally deep, bass-heavy, and warm when speaking within two inches of a directional microphone?
options: A) The electrical heating of the microphone's internal magnetic transformer
B) The physical slowing of sound waves passing through humid studio air
C) The digital distortion generated by computer audio recording software
D) 'Proximity Effect'—the artificial boost in low-frequency response that occurs in directional (pressure-gradient) microphones when the sound source is placed in close proximity to the capsule
questions.explanation: Pressure-gradient (cardioid/bidirectional) mics exhibit proximity effect: acoustic phase differences at close range artificially boost low frequencies (<200 Hz), creating intimate 'FM DJ voice'.

questions.sub_topic: Sound Bridge / Audio Bridge in Cinematic Continuity
questions.question: In cinematic editing, what is a 'Sound Bridge'?
options: A) An audio continuity device where sound from the previous scene carries over briefly into the next scene, or sound from the upcoming scene begins playing before the visual cut occurs
B) A physical steel bridge constructed inside a movie studio soundstage
C) A musical violin melody played during the opening studio logo animation
D) A specialized microphone cable that connects two movie theaters together
questions.explanation: A sound bridge connects two disparate visual scenes using contiguous audio, creating a smooth transition and rhythmic continuity across cuts.

questions.sub_topic: Mani Kaul and Kumar Shahani: Film Finance Corporation (FFC) New Wave
questions.question: Under the visionary chairmanship of B.K. Karanjia in the late 1960s, how did the Film Finance Corporation (FFC) catalyze the Indian New Wave cinema?
options: A) By purchasing one hundred percent of commercial Bollywood movie studios in Bombay
B) By offering modest state loans to talented FTII graduates (like Mani Kaul, Kumar Shahani, and Mrinal Sen) to make low-budget, artistic, non-commercial realistic films
C) By banning all foreign international films from being imported into Indian movie theaters
D) By funding high-budget commercial Hollywood action blockbusters shot in Europe
questions.explanation: The FFC (later NFDC) revitalized Indian cinema by financing low-budget auteur cinema (starting with Mrinal Sen's 'Bhuvan Shome', 1969), launching the Indian New Wave.

questions.sub_topic: Laura Mulvey: Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema (Male Gaze, 1975)
questions.question: In her landmark 1975 feminist film essay 'Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema', Laura Mulvey applied Freudian and Lacanian psychoanalysis to reveal that classical Hollywood cinema:
options: A) Promotes revolutionary socialist class consciousness among the urban working-class proletariat
B) Is structured around female matriarchal dominance over corporate movie studio executives
C) Is structured around the 'Male Gaze'—subordinating women characters to a passive erotic spectacle for the scopophilic pleasure of the active male protagonist and male spectator
D) Eliminates all narrative storytelling in favor of abstract optical mathematical patterns
questions.explanation: Mulvey decoded the 'male gaze': classical Hollywood cinema constructs women as passive sexualized spectacle (to-be-looked-at-ness), satisfying voyeuristic scopophilia and easing castration anxiety.

questions.sub_topic: Sergei Eisenstein: Dialectical Montage and Battleship Potemkin (1925)
questions.question: In his theory of montage, why did Sergei Eisenstein reject Pudovkin's concept of editing as 'linkage of bricks', defining montage instead as 'Collision' (Collision of Thesis and Antithesis)?
options: A) He believed that editing should be invisible and seamless so audiences never notice cuts
B) He insisted that all motion pictures should be shot in a single unbroken ninety-minute take
C) He argued that actors should be replaced with wooden mechanical marionettes in every scene

D) He argued that meaning arises dynamically from the conflict, collision, and clash of two opposing shots (thesis + antithesis = synthesis), sparking an intellectual and emotional shock in the spectator's mind
questions.explanation: Eisenstein drew on Marxist Hegelian dialectics: montage is not peaceful linkage (Pudovkin), but conflict and collision between juxtaposed shots that produces a new conceptual synthesis.

questions.sub_topic: André Bazin: Deep Focus and Long Take vs Montage
questions.question: Why did French theorist André Bazin champion 'Deep Focus' cinematography (Gregg Toland in 'Citizen Kane') and the 'Long Take' over Soviet montage editing?
options: A) Deep focus preserves spatial continuity and temporal duration, respecting the ambiguity of reality and granting the viewer freedom of choice to explore the frame, whereas montage imposes an authoritarian, manipulated meaning
B) Deep focus allowed movie cameras to shoot in total darkness without using any lighting
C) Deep focus was sixty percent cheaper to process in photochemical developing laboratories
D) Deep focus converted motion pictures into written literary novels on screen
questions.explanation: Bazin argued deep focus and long takes respect the integrity of physical reality and spectator autonomy, contrasting with montage's coercive, pre-chewed psychological manipulation.

questions.sub_topic: Ritwik Ghatak: Epic Cinema and Partition Trauma (Meghe Dhaka Tara, 1960)
questions.question: In Ritwik Ghatak's tragic masterpiece 'Meghe Dhaka Tara' (The Cloud-Capped Star, 1960), how does the famous sound design in the climax (the cracking sound of the whip) function symbolically?
options: A) It was an accidental microphone defect that the audio recording engineer forgot to erase

B) It ruptures realistic sound space with an expressionist sonic metaphor of brutal socio-economic exploitation and the deep trauma of the Bengal Partition, as Neeta cries 'Dada, ami baachte chai' ('Brother, I want to live')
C) It signifies that a physical horse-drawn carriage has arrived outside the hospital sanatorium
D) It was a commercial advertising jingle inserted to promote leather manufacturing goods
questions.explanation: Ghatak used melodrama and Brechtian distancing: the expressionistic whiplash sound effect externalizes Neeta's agony and the violent, agonizing trauma of the 1947 Bengal Partition.

questions.sub_topic: Digital Footprint Definition
questions.question: The permanent trail of identifiable digital data, browsing history, social media posts, and online activity left behind by an individual when using the internet is their:
options: A) Masthead
B) Cutline
C) Digital footprint
D) Byline
questions.explanation: A digital footprint encompasses active data (posts, emails) and passive telemetry (IP logs, cookies, clickstreams) recorded during internet use.

questions.sub_topic: Confirmation Bias in Social Media Consumption
questions.question: In cognitive psychology and social media consumption, how does 'Confirmation Bias' distort how users evaluate political news in their feeds?
options: A) Users verify every single news claim by consulting printed encyclopedias in libraries
B) Users automatically believe the exact opposite of whatever their family members believe
C) Users refuse to read any news article that contains more than one hundred words
D) Users actively seek out, believe, and share news stories that validate their pre-existing beliefs, while dismissing, ignoring, or attacking verified facts that challenge their worldview
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias leads individuals to selectively process information: eagerly embracing confirmatory evidence while rejecting discordant facts, supercharging polarization.

questions.sub_topic: Shoshana Zuboff: The Age of Surveillance Capitalism (Behavioral Futures Markets, 2019)
questions.question: In Shoshana Zuboff's foundational theory ('The Age of Surveillance Capitalism', 2019), what are 'Behavioral Futures Markets'?
options: A) Proprietary algorithmic markets where tech monopolies sell predictions of what human beings will do now, soon, and later to corporate business buyers seeking to modify and guarantee consumer behavior
B) Agricultural commodity markets where farmers trade physical contracts for future wheat deliveries
C) Stock exchanges where software engineers buy shares in computer hardware factories
D) Government auctions where telecommunications companies bid on radio broadcast frequencies
questions.explanation: Zuboff defined Behavioral Futures Markets: platforms extract behavioral surplus to train predictive machine intelligence, selling guaranteed predictions of future user actions to corporate buyers.

questions.sub_topic: Franco 'Bifo' Berardi: Semio-Capitalism and Info-Labor Exhaustion
questions.question: In his critique of the 24/7 digital attention economy ('The Soul at Work', 2009), Italian theorist Franco 'Bifo' Berardi argues that 'Semio-Capitalism' exploits human beings by:
options: A) Forcing factory laborers to physically mine coal deposits beneath the earth's surface

B) Putting the human soul, language, affect, and cognitive mental energy to work around the clock, causing mass psychic burnout, anxiety panic, and catastrophic exhaustion of the collective nervous system
C) Requiring all citizens to surrender their physical paper currency to private banks
D) Prohibiting human beings from using electrical home appliances during evening hours
questions.explanation: Berardi showed semio-capitalism mobilizes linguistic and affective capacities for economic valorization; the endless flood of info-stimuli overwhelms the neuro-psychic limits of human attention.

questions.sub_topic: Cory Doctorow: The 'Enshittification' of Digital Platforms (2023)
questions.question: In digital platform economics, how does tech critic Cory Doctorow describe the systematic three-stage lifecycle of platform degradation known as 'Enshittification'?
options: A) Platforms start as non-profit charities, then become municipal post offices, then convert into private banks
B) Platforms are built with high-quality silicon chips, which slowly corrode due to physical humidity and dust

C) First, platforms are good to their users to lock them in; second, they abuse users to make things good for their business customers (advertisers); third, they abuse business customers to claw back all value for the platform's shareholders until the platform dies
D) Platforms operate in English, then switch to Latin, then convert all user profiles into ancient Greek
questions.explanation: Doctorow's widely acclaimed framework: platforms start by subsidizing users to capture market share, pivot to squeeze users for business advertisers, and finally extract all surplus for shareholders.

questions.topic: Social Media: Platform Governance and Law
questions.sub_topic: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996): The Twenty-Six Words
questions.question: Why is Section 230(c)(1) of the US Communications Decency Act of 1996 celebrated by cyber-scholars as 'the twenty-six words that created the internet'?
options: A) It declares that the World Wide Web is the sovereign property of the United Nations
B) It legally bans commercial advertising from being published on social networking websites
C) It requires every computer programmer in the world to register their software code in Washington

D) It immunizes interactive computer services from being treated as the publisher or speaker of information provided by third-party users, shielding platforms from catastrophic liability for user-generated content
questions.explanation: Section 230(c)(1) states: 'No provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of any information provided by another information content provider,' birthright of UGC.

questions.sub_topic: Augmented Reality (AR) vs Virtual Reality (VR)
questions.question: What is the technical and experiential difference between 'Augmented Reality' (AR) and 'Virtual Reality' (VR)?
options: A) AR superimposes digital computer graphics and data onto the real physical world (like Pokémon GO or heads-up displays); VR completely replaces the real world with a fully simulated, immersive digital environment
B) AR requires wearing heavy diving suits underwater, while VR operates exclusively in airplanes
C) AR can only be experienced on radio, while VR is experienced exclusively in print newspapers
D) AR operates without any electricity, while VR consumes the electrical power of an entire city
questions.explanation: AR overlays computer-generated sensory elements onto the user's view of the physical world; VR provides full digital immersion, occluding the physical environment.

questions.sub_topic: Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) Function
questions.question: In World Wide Web design and development, what is the specific role of 'CSS' (Cascading Style Sheets) working alongside HTML?
options: A) It manages the physical routing of electrical power through underwater fiber optic internet cables
B) It controls the visual presentation, styling, layout, typography, colors, and responsive design of webpages, separating visual aesthetics from the underlying structural HTML content
C) It translates spoken English voice recordings into foreign languages automatically on web servers
D) It encrypts military satellite communications against foreign electronic intelligence interception
questions.explanation: CSS manages presentation (fonts, colors, layouts, grids, flexbox, responsiveness), separating graphic design styling from semantic HTML document structure.

questions.sub_topic: Lev Manovich: Database as a Symbolic Form (1999)
questions.question: In 'The Language of New Media' (2001), why does theorist Lev Manovich declare the 'Database' to be the dominant cultural form of the computer age, standing in direct opposition to the traditional 'Narrative'?
options: A) Databases can only store numbers, while narratives can only be written in rhyming poetry
B) Databases were invented by ancient Greek philosophers, while narratives were invented by Silicon Valley software engineers

C) Narrative constructs a linear, cause-and-effect trajectory of privileged events through time, whereas a database represents the world as an unstructured, non-hierarchical collection of items from which infinite trajectories can be assembled on demand
D) Databases are legally prohibited from containing any images, photographs, or audio files
questions.explanation: Manovich identified the database as modern media's new symbolic form: an open collection of records permitting varied algorithmic queries, challenging cinema and novelistic linear narrative causality.

questions.sub_topic: Alexander Galloway: Protocol - How Control Exists After Decentralization (2004)
questions.question: In 'Protocol: How Control Exists After Decentralization' (2004), how does Alexander Galloway disprove the utopian myth that the decentralized internet is free of control?
options: A) He proves that the internet is controlled by a single monarch who lives on an island in the Pacific Ocean
B) He shows that internet servers are physically controlled by municipal police officers in every neighborhood
C) He argues that computer microchips are designed to erase user data whenever a government election occurs

D) He proves that control has shifted to 'Protocols' (like TCP/IP and DNS)—rigid, non-negotiable sets of technical standards and code architectures that govern how data must flow across distributed networks
questions.explanation: Galloway argued protocol is to the digital network what discipline was to the factory: horizontal, non-negotiable technological rules (TCP/IP) that govern network possibility and enforce sovereign control.

questions.sub_topic: Lawrence Lessig: 'Code is Law' Doctrine (Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace, 1999)
questions.question: In his seminal cyberlaw text 'Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace' (1999), what fundamental reality does Lawrence Lessig capture with his iconic maxim 'Code is Law'?
options: A) In cyberspace, computer code, software architecture, and technical protocols constitute the ultimate regulator, dictating what users can and cannot do far more effectively and imperceptibly than traditional legislative legal statutes
B) All computer programmers must obtain law degrees and pass national bar association examinations
C) Written parliamentary laws are automatically translated into computer software code by artificial intelligence
D) Judicial courts are prohibited from reviewing any legal dispute that involves a personal computer
questions.explanation: Lessig's 'Code is Law' thesis: software architecture embedded in code regulates digital behavior directly by making certain actions physically impossible in cyberspace, outflanking statutory law.

questions.sub_topic: David Golumbia: The Cultural Logic of Computation (2009)
questions.question: In 'The Cultural Logic of Computation' (2009), linguist and digital theorist David Golumbia critiques 'Computationalism' as the dangerous ideological assumption that:
options: A) Computer processors should only be manufactured using natural biological tree wood materials
B) Human beings must stop using all forms of arithmetic in elementary school classrooms
C) Computers will permanently run out of mathematical numbers before the year 2050
D) All human thought, language, political structures, and social reality can and should be reduced to algorithmic calculation, logical processing, and computational machine logic
questions.explanation: Golumbia critiques computationalism: the ideology reducing complex human values, consciousness, language, and political institutions to mechanical algorithmic computation and rationalization.
